opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a useful analogy, but mostly for what it gets wrong, or at least for where it breaks down.

The standard story is that in the late nineties there was enormous investment in fiber and telecom infrastructure, far more than demand justified at the time. Lots of companies went bankrupt, investors lost a lot of money, and yet the infrastructure stayed in the ground and ended up being enormously valuable later. So people look at today's spending on data centers and GPUs and say: maybe this is the same, a bubble in the short run that builds something useful in the long run.

There are a few reasons I'm cautious about leaning on that too heavily.

First, the assets are very different. Fiber is extremely long-lived; you lay it once and it's useful for decades. GPUs depreciate quickly. A cluster built today is substantially less competitive in three or four years because the hardware improves so fast. So if demand doesn't show up in time, you don't get the "overbuilt infrastructure that's cheap to use later" dynamic in the same way. You end up with a lot of obsolete chips. The power, buildings and grid connections are more durable, and those may turn out to be the lasting part of the build-out.

Second, the demand picture is different. With telecom, a lot of the overinvestment came from wildly optimistic traffic projections that simply didn't materialize on the expected timeline. With AI, so far the compute is actually being used. Training runs absorb whatever is available, and inference demand has been growing very quickly. The open question isn't whether people will use the compute, but whether revenue will grow fast enough to justify the capital costs on the timescales investors expect.

Third, and I think most importantly, the ceiling is just much higher. The internet was a communication and distribution technology. It made existing activity more efficient and enabled new businesses, but it didn't substitute for human labor in a broad way. If AI systems become capable of doing a large share of the cognitive work in the economy, and eventually, with robotics, physical work, then the value at stake is a significant fraction of world GDP, which is on the order of tens of trillions of dollars per year in labor compensation alone. Against that, even a few trillion dollars of cumulative investment doesn't look excessive. It looks potentially small.

So I'd put it this way: the dot-com analogy is a reasonable reminder that individual companies and investors can lose a lot of money even when the underlying technology is transformative, and that timing really matters. There could well be corrections, and some players will overextend. But as an argument that the aggregate level of investment is irrational, I don't find it very convincing. If anything, if you take the possibility of broad automation seriously, the more surprising thing is how modest the investment still is relative to the potential payoff.

r001.rationale: It says AI could perform a large share of cognitive work and, with robotics, physical work, putting a significant share of world GDP in play.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the expectation of AI-driven growth acceleration today with expectations during the internet build-out.

r003.rationale: It says a few trillion dollars of AI investment may be modest relative to the potential payoff, but does not predict AI investment will far exceed economically justified internet infrastructure investment.

r004.rationale: It presents the internet build-out as investment that preceded later value, then frames AI spending as potentially a short-run bubble that builds useful infrastructure in the long run.

r005.rationale: It raises whether AI revenue will grow quickly enough to justify capital costs on investors’ expected timelines and says the potential payoff could make current investment look modest.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the analogy is actually quite informative, but you have to be careful about which lesson you draw from it. The common version of the story is that the late-nineties telecom build-out was a bubble: companies laid vastly more fiber than there was demand for, a lot of them went bankrupt, and investors lost enormous sums. And people point to that and say, look, we're doing the same thing with GPUs and data centers today.

But I think there are two things worth separating. One is whether the investment was socially valuable, and the other is whether the specific investors captured the returns. In the fiber case, the answer to the first question is pretty clearly yes. That dark fiber got lit up over the following decade and became the backbone for streaming, cloud computing, mobile internet, all of it. The investment was ahead of demand, but demand did arrive. The problem was mainly a timing and capture problem, not a problem of the underlying technology being overhyped.

Where I think the analogy breaks down a bit is on the economics of the asset itself. Fiber, once it's in the ground, lasts for decades, and the marginal cost of using it is close to zero. So you can overbuild and then wait. GPUs are different. They depreciate fast, both physically and because the next generation is substantially better. So if you build a hundred billion dollars of compute and the demand shows up five years late, a lot of that capital is just gone. That makes the AI build-out more sensitive to getting the timing right than the fiber build-out was.

The other difference, and I think this cuts in the other direction, is that the demand picture for AI looks more concrete to me than the demand picture for bandwidth did in 1999. Back then, you had to speculate about what people would do with all that capacity. With AI, we can already see models doing economically useful work, and we have fairly well-characterized scaling relationships telling us that more compute buys more capability. So the bet isn't purely speculative. The question is more about how quickly the capability translates into revenue, and whether the labs and hyperscalers making the investments are the ones who'll capture it.

So my overall read is: the analogy is a useful warning about who captures the value and about the risk of being early, but I'd be cautious about using it to argue that the investment itself is misguided. If anything, the infrastructure history suggests that overbuilding general-purpose capacity tends to look wasteful in the moment and foundational in retrospect.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI’s economic usefulness but does not identify flexible substitution for human labor as a reason for unusually large economic effects.

r002.rationale: It compares the demand picture for AI and bandwidth, but does not say AI gives stronger reason to expect growth acceleration than the internet did.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that eventual AI investment will exceed the economically justified internet infrastructure investment.

r004.rationale: It describes fiber investment as ahead of demand and says the key AI question is how quickly capability translates into revenue, conveying that AI investment may precede substantial revenue.

r005.rationale: It discusses whether AI investments will pay off, but does not explain that investment exceeding current AI revenue can reflect expectations of large future payoffs.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful analogy, particularly for separating two questions: whether a technology is going to be transformative, and whether the investments being made in it will earn a good return. Those can have quite different answers. You can be right about the importance of the internet and still invest too much in particular companies or infrastructure, or invest too early.

With AI, you could imagine something similar: a substantial build-out that turns out to be ahead of demand, but that also makes computing cheaper and enables valuable applications. So disappointing returns for investors wouldn’t necessarily imply that the technology itself was disappointing.

One important difference, though, is how long the infrastructure remains useful. Fiber can remain useful for a long time. AI chips could become economically obsolete much faster as newer, more efficient hardware arrives. That makes the timing of demand especially important. You need enough revenue while those assets are still competitive.

So I’d use the internet analogy as a way to think through possible outcomes, rather than as evidence that current AI investment must be either justified or a bubble. The crucial questions are how quickly demand grows, how much customers will pay, and how rapidly the infrastructure depreciates.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify AI’s ability to substitute flexibly for human labor as a source of unusually large economic effects.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the reason to expect AI-driven growth acceleration today with the reason during the internet build-out.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that AI investment will far exceed economically justified internet infrastructure investment.

r004.rationale: It says AI infrastructure could be built ahead of demand, but does not clearly connect the internet’s front-loaded infrastructure investment to AI investment preceding substantial AI revenue.

r005.rationale: It does not state that AI investment exceeding current revenue may reflect expectations of large future payoffs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful analogy, particularly because the internet build-out involved a lot of investment ahead of demand. You had firms laying fiber and building telecommunications infrastructure on the expectation that internet traffic would grow enormously. That expectation was broadly right, but it didn’t mean that every investment was profitable or that the timing was right.

There’s a similar distinction with AI. The technology could have a very large economic impact, while some of the companies investing in infrastructure earn disappointing returns. You have to distinguish the social value of the infrastructure from the returns captured by whoever finances it.

One important difference is how quickly the assets become obsolete. Fiber can remain useful for a long time, whereas an AI chip might become substantially less competitive within a few years. So you can’t necessarily build far ahead of demand and expect to wait for utilization to catch up. That makes the timing of investment, and the rate at which demand actually materializes, especially important.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI’s potential economic impact but does not identify flexible substitution for human labor as a reason for unusually large effects.

r002.rationale: It compares investment timing and asset obsolescence, but does not say growth acceleration is more likely from AI now than it was during the internet build-out.

r003.rationale: It makes no prediction that AI investment will eventually exceed economically justified internet infrastructure investment.

r004.rationale: It says internet infrastructure investment came ahead of demand and applies that timing concern to AI, noting that AI infrastructure might be built far ahead of demand.

r005.rationale: It mentions expectations of future demand and large AI economic impact, but does not state that AI investment exceeding current AI revenue can reflect expectations of large future payoffs.
